newsitem.title: FRANCE: Calls for ban on far-right French party fall flat.
newsitem.headline: Calls for ban on far-right French party fall flat.

text.p: Calls to ban the French extreme-right National Front have fallen flat, with party leader Jean-Marie Le Pen revelling in a barrage of denunciation over his public declaration that races are unequal.

Mainsteam politicians have savaged Le Pen in recent days for saying racial differences are a "fact", but they clearly fear stirring public sympathy with any attempt to punish him with anti-racism laws.

"France, cradle of human rights, is the world's only nation where a politician...can make racist statements, wallow in them and get a greater audience, instead of a trial or a ban," the Journal du Dimanche newspaper said in an editorial on Sunday.

Le Pen, who won 15 percent of the vote in 1995 presidential elections but whose party has no seats in parliament, has repeatedly hijacked national political debate towards his far-right agenda on races, immigration or jobs.
He wants to expel three million immigrants.

"Every day the facts show us that races are different," he said on Saturday, when he led a racially-charged march through the Mediterranean port of Marseille to denounce the death of a white teenager allegedly killed by an Arab youth.

Le Pen, a wily 68-year-old whose popularity feeds on controversy and fears about high unemployment, has said French civilisation is superior, but has stopped short of naming any supposedly "inferior" races.

Justice Minister Jacques Toubon said on Saturday that Le Pen's race remarks are too vague to be actionable by law. But he said he hoped the centre-right government would be ready to pass a draft bill to parliament next month to widen the legal definition of incitement to racial hatred and stiffen penalties.
Toubon and most other mainstream politicians have rejected calls to ban the National Front, floated last week by former Socialist leader Henri Emmanuelli.
Le Journal du Dimanche said a straw poll of jurists, sociologists and historians said the answer to the Front was to "fight without banning".
Successive governments have hoped to defuse the Front's lure by eradicating unemployment, but the latest dispute has revealed the emptiness of their arsenal.

Opinion polls indicate that Prime Minister Alain Juppe is unpopular with voters, perceived as out of touch with job worries and placing too much emphasis on economic austerity to qualify for a single European currency from 1999.
Le Pen, who routinely denounces any attempts to gag the Front as an attack on free speech, slammed Toubon's plan to tighten race-hatred laws as "grotesque".
He won more publicity on Sunday when anti-racism group MRAP and a left-wing journalists' union said it wanted French 3 television to scrap a planned interview with Le Pen late on Sunday night.
"One of Le Pen's greatest skills is to find scapegoats" for France's problems, said Pascal Perrineau, a leading sociologist.

Le Pen, whose slogan is "France for the French", has by turns exploited worries that foreigners are stealing French jobs, that Brussels bureaucrats are undermining sovereignty or that globalisation of the economy are destroying France.
The centre-right government and the Communist party feels threatened by the Front in the run-up to the 1998 legislative elections, since their voters are most vulnerable to Le Pen.
